context: The map shows data structures on the left, complexity analysis at the upper right, and algorithms at the lower right. The three sections have 7, 3, and 6 topic branches, respectively, for 16 in all. Lines show which section a topic belongs to. They do not prescribe a single reading order. The map gives no chapter numbers.

frames.explanation: The three tables below correspond to the three sections. Choose a section, then look up a topic by its row heading to find concepts, implementations, and example problems. The first row of the data structures table, also titled “Data structures,” is an overview branch.
frames.title: A map of the book

summary: Look up data structures, complexity analysis, and algorithms by topic.

tables.caption: Knowledge map: seven topics in data structures
rows: Data structures
Logical and physical structure, basic data types, number encoding, and character encoding.
Arrays and linked lists
Contiguous and noncontiguous storage, operations and their trade-offs, implementing a list with a dynamic array, and computer memory and caches.
Stacks and queues
Last-in, first-out stacks, first-in, first-out queues, double-ended queues, and implementing stacks and queues with arrays and linked lists.
Hash tables
How hash tables work and how to implement one with an array. Hash collisions, separate chaining, and open addressing. Uses and design goals of hash algorithms.
Trees
Perfect, complete, full, and balanced binary trees. Linked and array representations. Level-order, preorder, inorder, and postorder traversals. Binary search trees and AVL trees.
Heaps
Min-heaps, max-heaps, and priority queues. Implementing a heap with an array and building a heap. The top-k problem.
Graphs
Directed, connected, and weighted graphs. Adjacency lists versus adjacency matrices. Breadth-first and depth-first traversals.

tables.caption: Knowledge map: three topics in complexity analysis
rows: Iteration and recursion
For loops, while loops, and nested loops. The recursive call stack, tail recursion, and recursion trees. A comparison of iteration and recursion.
Time complexity
Asymptotic upper bounds of functions. Estimation methods and common growth rates. Worst-case, best-case, and average-case time complexity.
Space complexity
Estimation methods and common growth rates. Time–space trade-offs.

tables.caption: Knowledge map: six topics in algorithms
rows: Searching
Brute-force search (linear, breadth-first, and depth-first search), efficient search (binary search, hash lookup, and tree search), and choosing a search algorithm.
Sorting

Criteria include whether a sort is in-place, stable, adaptive, or comparison-based. The map groups the algorithms, in order, under “Repeated passes” (selection, bubble, and insertion sort), “Divide and conquer” (quicksort, merge sort, and heapsort), and “Non-comparison” (bucket, counting, and radix sort).
Divide and conquer
Problem characteristics and how to recognize them. Examples include binary search, constructing a tree, and the Tower of Hanoi.
Backtracking
Problem characteristics and a general code template. Examples include permutations, subset sum, and the n-queens problem.
Dynamic programming

Brute-force search, memoized recursion, and iterative recurrences. Overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, and independence from prior history once the state is known. Recognizing and solving dynamic programming problems. Examples include 0–1 knapsack, unbounded knapsack, and edit distance.
Greedy algorithms
Problem characteristics and steps toward a solution. Examples include fractional knapsack, maximum container capacity, and maximizing the product of an integer partition.

title: A map of the book
